analysis.one_liner: Moves decisions to prosecute serious military crimes, including sexual assault, out of the chain of command.
analysis.headline: With 222 cosponsors from both parties, the bill sat in the House Armed Services Committee for 18 months without ever getting a vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current military law, the officer in a service member's own chain of command decides whether charges for serious crimes like sexual assault, murder, and kidnapping are prosecuted, what kind of court-martial is used, and can even overturn a verdict. This bill would strip that power for the most serious offenses and give it to independent, experienced military lawyers outside the accuser's and accused's chain of command. It also adds sexual assault prevention training for officers, cadets, and service academies, requires better security measures like locks and cameras in barracks, and directs more specialized training for military prosecutors and investigators.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members who report sexual assault, domestic violence, or other serious crimes. Today they depend on the same chain of command that may include the accused, or the accused's superiors, to decide whether the case is prosecuted. The bill replaces that with independent convening authorities who are experienced prosecutors and outside the chain of command. It also strengthens prevention training for all officers above O-5 and senior enlisted leaders above E-9, cadets, and service academies, and requires surveys and upgrades of locks and cameras in military lodging and living spaces.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members reporting sexual assault and serious crimes

how_it_helps.text: For the most serious offenses, decisions on preferring, disposing of, and referring charges must be made by an officer in grade O-6 or higher who has significant court-martial trial experience and is outside the chain of command of the accused and the victim.

The bill covers offenses with a maximum sentence of more than one year of confinement, including sexual assault, murder, kidnapping, robbery, domestic violence offenses, child pornography, and their conspiracy, solicitation, and attempt offenses.

All uniformed officers and senior enlisted leaders must complete sexual assault prevention training equivalent to that given to victim advocates before promotion to O-5 or E-9, and training programs are expanded for cadets and service academies.
The Defense Department must survey all lodging and living spaces on military installations and run a program to replace or repair locks and install cameras to help prevent sexual assault.
Military prosecutors must receive enhanced, specialized training for handling sexual assault and domestic violence cases, and criminal investigator specialization is to be improved.

analysis.who_pays: The military services and their officer corps. Commanders lose direct control over whether serious criminal charges against people in their command are prosecuted, and each service must stand up a new office of convening authorities using existing personnel billets and funds, because the bill explicitly authorizes no new personnel or money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Military commanders' control over prosecution decisions

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes no additional personnel, billets, or funds, so the new offices of independent convening authorities and all training and security upgrades must be carried out using resources already authorized by law, which could strain existing units.

The good-faith objection from military leaders is that commanders need authority over prosecution to maintain good order and discipline in their units; the bill keeps that authority for minor offenses but removes it for a broad list of serious crimes, including murder, robbery, and kidnapping, not just sexual assault.
The changes take effect only one year after enactment, so any protection for current cases depends entirely on the Defense Department completing its policy revisions on time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and specific: a service member who reports sexual assault would no longer have her or his own chain of command deciding whether the case ever goes to trial, which was the central complaint in the Vanessa Guillén case and years of Pentagon data showing most victims don't report. The cost is mostly institutional, not financial: commanders lose leverage over prosecution of serious crimes, though they keep it for minor offenses. The main design weaknesses are the unfunded mandate for a new system and the broad coverage of non-sexual offenses, which critics argued went further than necessary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a markup or floor vote, and it expired there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Jackie Speier introduced the bill on June 23, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Armed Services.
The bill attracted 222 cosponsors, including 206 House Democrats and 16 House Republicans, but the committee took no further action on it.
The action history shows only two steps — introduction and referral to committee — with no markup, no report, and no floor vote for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The military chain of command kept its power to decide which serious criminal cases get prosecuted. In a widely reported follow-up, Congress did adopt the bill's central idea a few months later through a compromise in the fiscal 2022 defense authorization bill, creating independent special trial counsel for sexual assault and related offenses, while leaving commanders more authority than this bill would have.

for.name: Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill naming it after Vanessa Guillén, a soldier who was killed in 2020 after reportedly being sexually harassed, and pressed to move prosecution decisions out of the chain of command.

for.name: 206 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the large majority of the caucus.

for.name: 16 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from the start, including senior Armed Services member Mike Turner of Ohio.

against.name: House Committee on Armed Services
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Adam Smith (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out: no markup, no committee vote, and no request for a floor vote during the roughly 18 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Adam Smith
against.what_they_did: Publicly argued against fully removing commanders from decisions on courts-martial, favoring a more limited change, and the committee he chaired never acted on the bill.

against.name: Military service leadership
against.role: Joint Chiefs of Staff and service secretaries
against.what_they_did: Testified and spoke publicly in 2021 against taking court-martial convening authority away from commanders, which shaped the committee's reluctance to act on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from introduction: 206 of the cosponsors were Democrats and 16 were Republicans, so the bill's death in committee was not a party-line defeat.

industries.industry: Military officer corps and chain of command
industries.note: The bill would have taken away commanders' power to decide whether serious criminal charges, including sexual assault, go to trial — a power that lets an accused's own superiors make or block charging decisions. That loss of discretion is exactly what victims' advocates sought and military leadership resisted.

industries.industry: Military legal system (judge advocates and defense counsel)
industries.note: Prosecutors would gain a professionalized system with specialized training and independent convening authorities, while defense counsel would face an established prosecutorial office rather than ad hoc command decisions. Service members on both sides of a case would deal with career legal professionals instead of line commanders.
